standard.title: First Nations enterprise
standard.description: how First Nations Australian businesses and entrepreneurs develop opportunities in the market
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand the reasons businesses exist and characteristics of entrepreneurs (AC9HE7K02, AC9HE7K03). They have context from AC9HE8K02 on how businesses identify market opportunities and adapt.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate how First Nations Australian businesses and entrepreneurs develop opportunities in the market.

nodes.label: First Nations business structures and partnerships
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how First Nations Australian businesses and entrepreneurs establish partnerships or cooperatives to provide goods and services, including in sectors such as farming, fashion, design or tourism.
nodes.minimum_width: Investigate one First Nations Australian business or cooperative and explain how it is structured, what goods or services it provides, and how partnerships or collective arrangements support it.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate how First Nations Australian businesses establish partnerships or cooperatives to provide goods and services across different sectors (farming, fashion, design, cultural tourism). Explain how collective and partnership models reflect community values alongside commercial operation.
wider: Compare the cooperative business model used by some First Nations communities with mainstream investor-owned business structures, examining what each optimises for (profit, community benefit, cultural maintenance)

Investigate how Indigenous Land Use Agreements (ILUAs) and native title mechanisms have enabled First Nations businesses to enter markets in land management, environmental services and resource sectors
Research a First Nations fashion or design business and investigate how intellectual property and cultural ownership questions intersect with commercial activity
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not understand that First Nations businesses operate through distinct structural models (cooperatives, community enterprises, partnerships grounded in communal obligation) will misread the next node — treating participation in contemporary markets as identical to mainstream business participation rather than understanding the additional barriers and distinctive strategies involved.

response_modes.reason: Students may default to evaluating First Nations businesses against mainstream profit-maximising norms. Structured reasoning about different business purposes — community benefit, cultural maintenance, economic participation — establishes the frame needed before market participation is examined.

success_criteria: Identifies a specific First Nations Australian business or cooperative and describes its structure
Explains how the partnership or cooperative arrangement supports the provision of goods or services in that business

nodes.label: Participation in contemporary markets
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how First Nations Australian communities participate in contemporary markets, including how they produce, buy and sell goods and services and the strategies they use to overcome difficulties in accessing markets.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain one way that a First Nations Australian community or business participates in a contemporary market, and identify at least one difficulty they face in accessing that market.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how First Nations Australian communities participate in contemporary markets: producing, buying and selling goods and services; approaches to marketing, employment and social contribution; and strategies used to overcome difficulties in accessing markets (e.g. remoteness, capital access, cultural protocols in business contexts).
wider: Investigate how digital platforms and e-commerce have opened new market access pathways for First Nations businesses in remote and regional areas that face geographic barriers to mainstream markets
Research the role of organisations such as Supply Nation in supporting First Nations businesses to access government and corporate procurement markets
Examine how tourism provides economic participation opportunities for First Nations communities and the tensions between commercial tourism and cultural and environmental custodianship

response_modes.reason: First Nations market participation spans urban businesses, remote community enterprises, cultural tourism, and digital trade. Multiple contexts prevent students from treating one case study as representative of a diverse and geographically varied economic reality.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations market participation contexts are genuinely diverse — remote agriculture, urban creative industries, cultural tourism, environmental services. Each context surfaces different participation strategies and different barriers, offering rich comparative inquiry that connects economics to geography, history and civics.
success_criteria: Describes at least one way a First Nations community or business participates in a contemporary market
Identifies at least one barrier to market access and explains a strategy used to address it

nodes.label: Connection to Country as economic innovation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how First Nations Australian businesses and entrepreneurs use connection to, and responsibility for, Country/Place to make innovations in the production and distribution of goods and services.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe one example of a First Nations business innovation that draws on knowledge of, or responsibility for, Country/Place — such as medicines, food products, environmental services or cultural tourism — and explain how Country/Place connection is central to the innovation.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how First Nations Australian businesses and entrepreneurs use connection to Country/Place as the basis for innovation in production and distribution, including examples such as bush food and medicine products, cultural tourism, environmental monitoring, and design. Explain how this knowledge creates market value while maintaining cultural obligations.
wider: Investigate the bush food and native ingredient industry in Australia — how First Nations knowledge of plants and their uses is being commercialised, and what intellectual property, benefit-sharing and cultural authority questions this raises

Research how First Nations-led environmental and conservation enterprises (e.g. carbon farming, ranger programs, fire management) generate income from Country/Place knowledge in ways that integrate economic and custodial responsibilities

Compare how connection to Country as an economic asset is legally recognised and protected (e.g. through native title, geographic indications, cultural heritage law) versus how it remains vulnerable to appropriation without adequate protection

response_modes.reason: Country/Place connection as economic innovation is genuinely diverse — food, medicine, tourism, environmental services, design. Multiple contexts prevent reduction to a single example and reveal the breadth of economic activity grounded in this relationship.

success_criteria: Identifies a specific First Nations business innovation that draws on Country/Place knowledge or connection
Explains how the innovation creates market value while reflecting responsibilities to Country/Place
